items.headline: The hidden scale-out problem behind CAR-T’s growth
items.preview: CAR-T therapies like Carvykti face unique manufacturing challenges as demand grows.
items.article:
At the Raritan, New Jersey, facility where Legend Biotech and Johnson & Johnson manufacture Carvykti, a multiple myeloma patient named Colleen met some of the employees who had worked on the CAR-T cell therapy she received while battling for her life.
It was a meeting that showcased the deep personal connection patients have to CAR-T therapies, Legend said. And for the company, it also laid bare the therapy’s unique operating model: A commercial dose is not just tied to a product. It is tied to one patient.
Carvykti’s commercial footprint is expanding quickly. First approved in 2022, the treatment notched $657 million in second-quarter net trade sales, 50% above the year-earlier period, and is available at 348 sites across 19 markets.
Why this matters: As demand grows, the manufacturing challenge is not simply making a bigger batch. Patient cells, manufacturing slots, quality testing, release dates, logistics and treatment center schedules all have to move together. Legend has spent years building that wider system around Carvykti, ensuring that growth depends on adding volume without losing reliability.

items.headline: Mutant p53 drives ferroptosis resistance through metabolic plasticity in pancreatic cancer
items.preview: Research reveals how mutant p53 protects pancreatic cancer cells from ferroptosis.
items.article:
Pancreatic cancer is one of the deadliest malignancies known to medicine, and its resistance to virtually every conventional therapy has long frustrated oncologists worldwide. Now, a team of researchers at the University of Verona in Italy has uncovered a mechanism that helps explain why pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, or PDAC, is so stubbornly difficult to kill—and, crucially, how that defense might be dismantled.
Why this matters: The findings suggest that combining ferroptosis-inducing drugs with agents that restore normal p53 function could open a powerful new front against this aggressive disease. The study demonstrates that mutant versions of the p53 protein actively protect tumor cells from ferroptosis, an iron-dependent form of cell death, highlighting a potential therapeutic vulnerability.

items.headline: Ionis’ rare neurology drug approved; Pfizer inks an ADC deal
items.preview: Ionis Pharmaceuticals receives FDA approval for a drug targeting Alexander disease.
items.article:
The Food and Drug Administration on Thursday approved the first medicine for an extremely rare, often fatal neurological condition known as Alexander disease. Developed by Ionis Pharmaceuticals, Zanvastro works by reducing the production of a protein that forms toxic clumps damaging the nervous system.
Why this matters: This approval marks Ionis' first independent product launch from its neurology pipeline and is expected to improve stability in patients. Additionally, Pfizer has entered a co-development agreement with Medicus Pharma for an antibody drug conjugate targeting melanotransferrin, expanding its oncology portfolio.

items.headline: Organoid co-cultures expose epithelial and fibroblast diversity in pancreatic cancer and pancreatitis
items.preview: New organoid models reveal interactions between pancreatic cancer cells and fibroblasts.
items.article:
Pancreatic cancer has long been one of the most formidable opponents in oncology, and a substantial part of its lethality lies not in the cancer cells themselves but in the tissue that surrounds them. Researchers have built a multi-stromal organoid co-culture platform that reveals how pancreatic epithelial cells and fibroblasts reshape one another in disease.
Why this matters: This model allows for a better understanding of the complex interactions in pancreatic cancer and pancreatitis, potentially leading to more effective therapies by capturing the heterogeneity of the tumor microenvironment.

items.headline: Hyperglycemic stress aggravates diabetic retinopathy and nephropathy
items.preview: Study reveals mechanisms linking ciliary dysfunction to diabetic complications.
items.article:
Primary cilia are essential microtubule-based sensory organelles, and their dysfunction has been increasingly linked to metabolic stress. A study reveals that ciliary defects in retinal photoreceptors and renal tubules exacerbate tissue damage during diabetic complications.
Why this matters: The findings uncover a reciprocal regulatory mechanism that drives cilium disassembly under hyperglycemic stress, providing promising therapeutic targets for the treatment of metabolic ciliopathies, particularly in diabetic retinopathy and nephropathy.
